nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in formal writing, policy discussions and legal or political commentary to say an action is unwise for the situation. In everyday speech they usually say 'not a good idea' or 'not smart.' It is often softer than 'wrong,' which implies ethical failure.

distinctions.note: 'Inadvisable' is more common in everyday professional speech and simply means not recommended. 'Inexpedient' implies the action fails to achieve its purpose.
'Unethical' concerns morality. 'Inexpedient' concerns practical wisdom, even if the action is morally acceptable.

examples.everyday: Buying a second car right now seems inexpedient, since we just paid off the first one.
examples.professional: Changing the database schema during the release freeze is inexpedient, so let's postpone it.
examples.analytical: The senator argued that the bill was legally sound but politically inexpedient at that moment.

nuance.analogy: Like taking the highway during rush hour when a side road would get you there faster.
nuance.etymology: From in- 'not' and expedient, from Latin expedire 'to free from hindrance, to be advantageous'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'inexperience' or 'inexpensive'.
Using it to mean unethical; it refers to practical unwisdom.

senses.definition: The ability to solve difficult problems in original, clever, and inventive ways; ingeniousness.
senses.example: The pyramids demonstrate the ingenuity of the ancient Egyptians.

senses.definition: An ingenuous action or thought.
Ingenuousness; honesty, straightforwardness.

core.definition: Skill in solving problems or creating clever new solutions, often in original and inventive ways.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NOO, with a secondary stress on in. The second syllable is weak, and the final -ity is a short ee sound. Learners often stress the last syllable or pronounce the middle as jen.

nuance.connotation: positive, since it praises creative problem solving
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ingenuity to praise practical, creative problem solving, as in American ingenuity or show ingenuity. It is common in business, engineering, and news writing. In everyday talk, people might say creative or clever, but ingenuity sounds natural when giving praise.

distinctions.note: Creativity is the ability to make something new, while ingenuity emphasizes clever problem solving under constraints.
Ingenuousness means innocent frankness, not inventiveness, so the two are unrelated in meaning despite the similar spelling.

examples.everyday: It took some real ingenuity to fix the car with just duct tape and a coat hanger.
examples.professional: Her ingenuity in reusing old hardware saved the team a large part of the budget.
examples.analytical: Hume suggests that human ingenuity arises from the mind's ability to combine known ideas in new ways.

nuance.analogy: Ingenuity is like a chef making a satisfying meal from leftovers, turning limited ingredients into something clever and useful.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ingenuitas, from ingenuus, native, free-born, or from ingenium, mind, talent.
common_mistakes: Confusing ingenuity with ingenuousness, which means innocence or frankness.
Putting the stress on the last syllable, as in in-juh-noo-uh-TEE.

senses.definition: Characterized by the creation of new ideas or inventions.
Forward-looking; ahead of current thinking.

core.definition: Using new ideas or methods; creative and ahead of how things are usually done.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, IN. The middle 'uh' is reduced, and the final '-tive' is short, like 'tiv', not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises creativity and originality. It may sound like marketing language when used about ordinary products.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly in business, product descriptions, and everyday praise: 'an innovative solution' or 'a really innovative idea.' It is friendly and positive, though in casual talk 'creative' or 'cool' may be more natural.

distinctions.note: Creative stresses imagination in making things; innovative stresses making a new idea practical or changing how things are done.
New only means recent or not existing before; innovative implies the newness is clever and valuable.

examples.everyday: That new app for splitting dinner bills is really innovative, you should try it.
examples.professional: We're looking for an innovative approach to reduce model training time without losing accuracy.
examples.analytical: Her argument is innovative because it reframes the problem as one of trust rather than of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a new route across a familiar mountain that makes the trip shorter and more interesting.
nuance.etymology: From innovate plus the suffix -ive, from Latin innovare, 'to renew.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'in-no-VAY-tive.'
Using it to mean 'new' in a neutral way, as in 'an innovative store opened on my street' when nothing new is actually being done.

senses.definition: Excessive; unreasonable or inappropriate in magnitude.

core.definition: Much larger, greater, or longer than is reasonable or necessary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, AWR, with a strong American 'r'. The final syllable is a reduced 'it', not 'ate'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies excess that is unreasonable or unjustified, often used for time, money, or attention.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in formal writing and complaints: 'an inordinate amount of time.' In casual speech people say 'way too much' or 'a ton of.' It is a polished word that sounds slightly stiff in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Excessive is the general word for too much; inordinate suggests a lack of reasonable limit, often in a formal complaint.
Extreme describes the degree or outer edge; inordinate describes something that is out of proportion to what's reasonable.

examples.everyday: The repair shop took an inordinate amount of time, and I still don't have my car back.
examples.professional: The project is taking an inordinate amount of compute, so we need to review the training schedule.
examples.analytical: The author gives inordinate weight to a single anecdote, which distorts the broader argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a bowl of soup that's so salty it's no longer a meal but a problem.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inordinatus, from in- 'not' plus ordinatus 'arranged, ordered,' from ordo 'order.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'in-OR-di-nate' with the final syllable stressed or as 'ate'.
Confusing it with 'ordinary' because of the shared root; inordinate means excessive, not regular.

inordinate.etymology: From Middle English *inordinat*, from Latin *inōrdinātus* (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from *in-* + *ordinatus*, past participle of *ōrdinō* (“to arrange, order”).

senses.definition: Without any delay; in an instantaneous manner.

core.definition: Happening at once, with no delay at all; immediately, in the same moment.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TAY, the third syllable of six, and the 'ee-us' ending is quick. The word is pronounced 'in-stun-TAY-nee-us-lee', so avoid stressing the 'tan' sound as 'TAN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and slightly formal, and it is usually used to emphasize speed or the absence of delay.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'instantaneously' mainly in technical, scientific, or formal writing, and they usually choose 'instantly' or 'right away' in everyday speech. It can sound stiff in casual conversation, as in 'I instantaneously knew', where 'immediately' or 'right away' is more natural. In software and engineering, 'instantaneously' is often used when a system responds without any lag.

distinctions.note: Instantly is the everyday word for immediately, while instantaneously is more formal and emphasizes a truly simultaneous or lag-free event.
Immediately can mean soon, with a short wait, while instantaneously implies no delay at all.
Quickly describes speed over time, while instantaneously describes an event that happens at a single instant.

examples.everyday: The lights came on instantly when I flipped the switch, which was nice after the long power outage.
examples.professional: The alert fires instantaneously when the threshold is crossed, so there is no batch delay in the pipeline.
examples.analytical: A signal that propagates instantaneously is an idealization that relativity forbids, which makes it a useful thought experiment.

nuance.analogy: Like a light switch and a bulb: the connection is so immediate that you cannot see any gap between the two actions.
nuance.etymology: From instantaneous, from Medieval Latin instantaneus, from Latin instans 'present, immediate'.
common_mistakes: Using 'instantaneously' in everyday speech, where 'instantly' or 'right away' sounds more natural.
Stressing the 'tan' syllable; the main stress is on the 'tay' syllable.

senses.definition: The point of interconnection between systems or subsystems.
senses.example: The data is sent over the air interface to the remote system.

senses.definition: The connection between a user and a machine.
senses.example: The options are selected via the user interface.

senses.definition: In some languages, a block of code declaring the interface (point of interconnection) between a class and code that interacts with it.
The point of interconnection or contact between entities.
senses.example: Public relations firms often serve as the interface between a company and the press.

senses.definition: The connection between parts of software; also the public or published sections of an object or module.
senses.example: This interface is implemented by several Java classes.

senses.definition: In object-oriented programming, a piece of code defining a set of operations that other code must implement.
senses.example: The Audio and Video classes both implement the IPlayable interface.

senses.definition: The internal surface of a coiled protein (compare exoface).
A thin layer or boundary between different substances or two phases of a single substance.
senses.example: If water and oil are mixed together, they tend to separate, and at equilibrium they are in different strata with an oil-water interface in between.

senses.definition: To construct an interface for.
To connect through an interface.
To serve as an interface.
To meet for discussion.
senses.example: Let's interface on Wednesday.

core.definition: The point or system where two parts, or a person and a machine, connect and interact, such as a screen or menu.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, IN, and the middle syllable is reduced to 'ter'. The last syllable rhymes with 'place', so pronounce it 'fayss' with a clear s, not 'fayse'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In everyday use it refers to screens and menus; in technical use it is a precise term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'interface' for phones, computer screens, software menus, and business systems, often casually ('the new interface is easier'). In work settings, 'interface with' means to communicate or work with another person or team, as in 'I'll interface with the finance team.' In technical contexts it is more precise and can refer to code.

distinctions.note: An API is a specific set of rules for programs to communicate; an interface is the general point of connection and can be a screen, a protocol, or an API.
Front end usually means the client-side code or the part users see; interface is broader and can mean any point of connection.

examples.everyday: I can't figure out the new interface on my banking app; the buttons moved around again.
examples.professional: The payments service exposes a clean interface, so the mobile team can integrate without knowing the database schema.
examples.analytical: The class defines a public interface that hides the implementation, which makes the component easier to test and replace.

nuance.analogy: Like the plug and socket between a lamp and the wall: the shape of the connection matters more than what happens inside each device.
nuance.etymology: From inter- (between) plus face, from Latin facies 'form, surface'.
common_mistakes: Using 'interface' as a verb with the wrong preposition; say 'interface with a system' or 'interface between two systems'.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress falls on IN.

senses.definition: In an inward manner; to or toward the inside or to oneself.
senses.example: Jacob groaned inwardly when he was called on to answer the question.

core.definition: In your private thoughts or feelings, without showing it outwardly; or toward the inside.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The 'ard' sound in the middle is a reduced 'urd', and the final -ly is a short 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It often suggests hidden emotion, such as anger or relief that is not visible to others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'inwardly' to describe feelings you keep private, such as 'I was inwardly furious but smiled anyway.' It is common in both speech and writing. In casual talk, people often say 'on the inside' or 'in my head' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Internally' is more technical and often refers to organs or systems; 'inwardly' refers to private feelings or thoughts.
'Privately' means in private or out of public view; 'inwardly' means in your mind, even if you say nothing.

examples.everyday: My boss said the project was fine, but I was inwardly relieved it was over.
examples.professional: I was inwardly frustrated when the meeting ran over, but I kept my comments short.
examples.analytical: The poem's speaker is outwardly silent but inwardly in conflict, and that tension drives the whole argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a lamp lit behind a frosted shade: the glow is real, but only faintly visible from outside.
nuance.etymology: From inward plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confuse 'inwardly' with 'internally' when talking about feelings; use 'inwardly' for private thoughts.
Misspell it as 'inwardlly' with a double l.

senses.definition: Admitting no return; from or by which one cannot return.
senses.example: an irremeable way

core.definition: Having no way back; from or through which one cannot return.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on REM, and the word has four syllables: ih-REM-ee-uh-buhl. The -ee- is a clear long e, and the final -able reduces to 'uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somber. It suggests a path or passage with no return, often in poetic or elevated writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation; you will meet it in older poetry, classic literature, or scholarly writing. In everyday speech, say 'one-way' or 'no way back.' It is a rare literary word, so use it only when writing with a deliberately elevated tone.

distinctions.note: Irreversible is common and means cannot be reversed; irremeable is rare and literary, and it refers specifically to a route with no return.
One-way is everyday and practical; irremeable is elevated and suggests something final or mysterious.

examples.everyday: Once you cross that river on the old map, you're on an irremeable path, so think carefully before you go.
examples.professional: Our migration plan is effectively irremeable, since the legacy database cannot be restored once we switch.
examples.analytical: Dante's descent into the underworld is figured as an irremeable passage, which marks the finality of the damned.

nuance.analogy: Like a one-way tunnel with no exit behind you: once inside, the only way is forward.
nuance.etymology: From Latin irremeabilis, from in- 'not' plus remeare 'to go back', from re- 'back' plus meare 'to go'.
common_mistakes: Using it in everyday speech where one-way or irreversible is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle syllables as separate sounds; reduce them to a quick schwa.

senses.definition: In AI: One update step of training, usually on one batch of data.
A single repetition of the code within such a repetitive process.
senses.example: The code calculates the appropriate value at each iteration.

senses.definition: The use of repetition in a computer program, especially in the form of a loop.
A recital or a second performance; a repetition.
A variation or version.
senses.example: The architect drafted several iterations of the floorplan before deciding on his final design.

core.definition: One repetition of a cycle in a repeated process; in AI training, one update step on one batch of data.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves from IT in the verb iterate to RAY in iteration, and the ending is a plain shun sound. Do not stress the first syllable or turn -tion into 'shee-un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise term used in technical and professional settings.
nuance.usage_note: In data science and AI, Americans use iteration for one pass of a loop or one update step during training; an epoch is a full pass through the whole dataset. In everyday speech it is rarely used; people say 'round' or 'version'. In meetings, 'the third iteration' means a version of a product or document.

distinctions.note: An epoch is one full pass through the whole training dataset; an iteration is one update step, often on one batch.
A version is a named release; an iteration is a development step that may never be shipped.

examples.everyday: This is our third iteration of the chili recipe, and I think it's finally right.
examples.professional: The model improved after each training iteration, so we logged the loss every fifty steps.
examples.analytical: Each iteration in a learning algorithm refines a belief, so convergence depends on the update rule as much as on the data.

nuance.analogy: Like a sculptor's pass over the stone, where each iteration removes a little more.
nuance.etymology: From Latin iteratio, 'repetition', from iterare, 'to repeat'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; say it-uh-RAY-shun, not IT-uh-ray-shun.
Using iteration for a finished version; in American business talk it usually means a draft or step in the process.

conversation.text: Each iteration processes one mini-batch and updates the weights once.
After three iterations of the labeling guidelines, annotator agreement finally improved.
The loop crashes on the last iteration because the final batch is smaller.

senses.definition: One of the bones, usually bearing teeth, which form the framework of the mouth.
The part of the face below the mouth.
senses.example: His jaw dropped in amazement.

senses.definition: Anything resembling the jaw (sense 1) of an animal in form or action; the mouth or way of entrance.
senses.example: the jaws of a pass; the jaws of darkness; the jaws of death.

senses.definition: A notch or opening.
A notched or forked part, adapted for holding an object in place.
senses.example: the jaw of a railway-car pedestal.

senses.definition: One of a pair of opposing parts which are movable towards or from each other, for grasping or crushing anything between them.
senses.example: the jaws of a vise; the jaws of a stone-crushing machine.

senses.definition: Impudent, abusive, or worthless talk.
An axle guard.
The curved part of the cushion marking the entry to the pocket.
The inner end of a boom or gaff, hollowed in a half circle so as to move freely on a mast.
To assail or abuse by scolding.
To scold; to clamor.
To talk; to converse.
(of a ball) To stick in the jaws of a pocket.

core.definition: Either of the two bony structures of the mouth that hold the teeth; the lower part of the face below the mouth.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with an open, rounded vowel, the same as in law or saw. Do not add a glide sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in anatomy and everyday talk. In informal speech, to jaw means to chat at length, which can sound a bit negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jaw for the body part in medical, everyday and sports contexts, such as a broken jaw or a punch to the jaw. The verb to jaw is informal and means to talk at length, often in a complaining way. Americans say jawbone for the bone itself in technical use.

distinctions.note: The chin is the front point of the lower face, while the jaw is the whole bony structure running back toward the ear.
Mandible is the technical term for the lower jawbone, while jaw is the everyday word for the structure.

examples.everyday: He took a punch to the jaw in the game but kept playing.
examples.professional: The dentist explained that the jaw pain was linked to the bite, not the teeth.
examples.analytical: The poet's image of a lion's jaw turns the sacred text into a place of danger.

nuance.analogy: A jaw is like the hinge and frame of a door: it holds the mouth in place and opens and shuts it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English jowe, related to Old French joue, cheek.
common_mistakes: Using jaw to mean the whole face instead of the lower part.
Saying JAW-ee as if it had two syllables.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word lechi (לֶחִי) means jaw or cheek, and Greek siagōn (σιαγών) is used for cheek in the New Testament. In Judges 15:15 (RSV) Samson uses the jawbone of an ass to defeat the Philistines. Ezekiel 29:4 (RSV) speaks of hooks placed in the jaws of a sea monster, a picture of God controlling the powerful.

jaw.etymology: From Middle English *jowe* (“jaw; sides of the lower face”), the further origin of which is.

senses.definition: A Hebrew personal name in the Old Testament, most notably the father of Elkanah and the grandfather of the prophet Samuel.

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name in the Old Testament, most notably the father of Elkanah and the grandfather of the prophet Samuel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'h' is pronounced lightly and the final syllable rhymes with 'Sam'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Jeroham almost only in biblical or church contexts, such as Bible study or teaching on the family of Samuel. It is not a common modern name.

examples.everyday: When we read 1 Samuel together, I always forget that Jeroham is Samuel's grandfather.
examples.professional: In the lesson plan, I start with Jeroham as the father of Elkanah so the class can trace Samuel's family line.
examples.analytical: The genealogy in 1 Samuel 1:1 places Jeroham as the father of Elkanah, a detail that frames Samuel's birth within a specific family lineage.

nuance.analogy: Like a name at the top of a family tree: he matters because the line flows through him.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yeroham, a name of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (jeh-ROH-ham).
Confusing Jeroham with Jeremiah or Jeremy.
nuance.biblical_note: Jeroham is the father of Elkanah in 1 Samuel 1:1, making him the grandfather of the prophet Samuel. He is a minor figure, but he anchors the family line that leads into the story of Hannah and the birth of Samuel. Other men named Jeroham appear in 1 Chronicles, mostly in genealogies.

senses.definition: To furnish someone with sufficient relevant information and include them in the decision-making process.

core.definition: To make sure someone gets the relevant information and is included in decisions as they happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOOP, the last word. Reduce "the" to a quick "thuh" before a consonant, and keep the "l" clear and light.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in offices and teams, often in the form "keep me in the loop" or "loop me in." It is friendly and slightly informal. A natural reply is "Thanks, I appreciate it" or "Will do."

distinctions.note: Keep in the loop is about receiving information about decisions; keep up is about staying at the same pace or level as others.
In the know describes someone who already has inside information; keep in the loop describes the act of giving someone that information.

collocations: keep the team in the loop

examples.everyday: Can you keep me in the loop about the weekend plans?
examples.professional: Please keep the client team in the loop on any schedule changes this week.
examples.analytical: A good governance structure keeps every stakeholder in the loop, so that decisions reflect the knowledge the whole organization holds.

nuance.analogy: Like being added to a group chat: you see every message as it happens and can respond before the decision is made.
common_mistakes: Saying "keep in loop" without the article "the."
Using "keep in the loop" to mean physically staying in a circle or cycle.

conversation.text: Please keep me in the loop on any changes to the launch date.
We need to keep the client in the loop, even if the news is bad.
Thanks for keeping me in the loop while I was out.

senses.definition: To work and press into a mass, usually with the hands; especially, to work, as by repeated pressure with the knuckles, into a well mixed mass, the materials of bread, cake, etc.
To treat or form as if by kneading; to beat.
Of cats, to make an alternating pressing motion with the two front paws.
To mix thoroughly; form into a homogeneous compound.
The act of kneading something.

core.definition: To press, fold, and stretch dough or other soft food with your hands until it is smooth and elastic.

pronunciation.tip: The k is silent, so start with the n sound. Use a long e vowel, and do not pronounce it like 'need' with a hard d sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a common cooking or craft action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use knead in everyday cooking, especially for bread, pizza dough, and pastry. Home cooks often say 'knead the dough for ten minutes.' In a kitchen with a stand mixer, people say 'mix on low with the dough hook' or 'knead it in the mixer' for the same action.

distinctions.note: Mixing combines ingredients together. Kneading is a specific pressing and folding action used to develop gluten in dough.
Stirring uses a spoon to combine wet ingredients. Kneading requires hands or a mixer hook and works a dough into a firm mass.

examples.everyday: Can you help me knead this dough? My wrists are getting tired.
examples.professional: In the bakery, we knead the dough in the mixer on low for about eight minutes before the first rise.
examples.analytical: Kneading develops gluten networks, which is why repeated pressing changes the texture of bread from sticky to elastic.

nuance.analogy: Kneading dough is like working a stiff clay until it becomes soft and ready to shape.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cnedan, meaning to knead or press together.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the k as a sound at the start.
Confusing knead with need in speech and writing.

knead.etymology: From Middle English *kneden*, from Old English *cnedan*, from **knedan*, from Proto-Germanic **knudaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **gnet-* (“to press together”).

conversation.text: Knead the dough for about ten minutes.
My grandma kneads bread by hand.
I kneaded the pizza dough until it was smooth.

senses.definition: Of or relating to lakes.

core.definition: Relating to lakes, or living in, formed in, or growing near a lake.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KUS. The 'r' is pronounced in American speech, and the final syllable is a short 'in' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It is precise and used mainly in science or scholarly writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lacustrine mainly in geology, biology, ecology, and literary description of lakeside landscapes. Ordinary speakers would say 'lake' or 'lakeside' instead. It is correct American usage but sounds technical in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Lakeside is everyday and simply means next to a lake, while lacustrine is technical and can describe organisms or deposits formed in lakes.
Riverine relates to rivers, while lacustrine relates to lakes; geologists use both terms to describe different depositional environments.

examples.everyday: We walked along the lacustrine trail near the lake and watched the herons.
examples.professional: The water sample came from a lacustrine habitat, so we need to adjust the salinity model.
examples.analytical: The researchers traced the lacustrine sediments to show that the basin held a freshwater lake for thousands of years.

nuance.analogy: Lacustrine is like 'marine' for lakes: it names the world of lakes in the way marine names the world of the sea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lacus, lake, with the suffix -ine, meaning relating to.
common_mistakes: Using it in everyday speech where 'lake' or 'lakeside' would be more natural.
Stressing the first syllable; the stress is on KUS.

senses.definition: Numerous; vast; very great in number.
senses.example: Russia’s labor and capital resources are woefully inadequate to overcome the state’s needs and vulnerabilities, which are legion.

senses.definition: A national organization or association of former servicemen, such as the American Legion.
A large number of people; a multitude.
senses.example: Their complicated affairs are managed by a legion of accountants.

senses.definition: A great number.
The major unit or division of the Roman army, usually comprising 3000 to 6000 infantry soldiers and 100 to 200 cavalry troops.

A combined arms major military unit featuring cavalry, infantry, and artillery, including historical units such as the British Legion, and present-day units such as the Spanish Legion and the French Foreign Legion.
A large military or semi-military unit trained for combat; any military force; an army, regiment; an armed, organized and assembled militia.
A group of orders inferior to a class; in scientific classification, a term occasionally used to express an assemblage of objects intermediate between an order and a class.
To form into legions.

core.definition: A very large number of people or things; a multitude.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'gi' is pronounced like the 'j' in 'jump', and the final syllable is a reduced 'jun', not 'jon'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to dramatic. It suggests an overwhelming or impressive number, sometimes with a playful tone.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people say 'tons of' or 'a ton of' instead, but 'legions of fans' or 'legions of critics' sounds lively in writing and speech. When capitalized, the American Legion is a veterans' organization, and Americans say 'the American Legion' with the article.

distinctions.note: Multitude is a plain, neutral word for a large crowd; legion adds a sense of an enormous, sometimes overwhelming, number.
An army is a military force; the figurative sense of legion means a huge number, not an organized fighting force.

examples.everyday: I've got a legion of emails to answer before the weekend.
examples.professional: We have a legion of tickets in the backlog, so let's prioritize the critical ones.
examples.analytical: The theologian faces a legion of interpretive questions that the text does not resolve.

nuance.analogy: Like an army marching in: the word brings to mind thousands of soldiers, each one a single unit of a much larger force.
nuance.etymology: From Latin legio, a levy or military unit, from legere 'to gather, choose'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it LEG-ee-un; the stress is on the first syllable with a soft j sound.
Using legion as a regular verb in everyday speech; the verb is rare and mostly literary.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament, legion (Greek legiōn, from Latin legio) is a Roman military unit of several thousand soldiers. In Mark 5:9 (RSV) the man possessed by unclean spirits says his name is 'Legion' because they are many, and Luke 8:30 repeats the name. In Matthew 26:53 Jesus says he could call on more than twelve legions of angels, a picture of vast heavenly power that he chooses not to use.

legion.etymology: Attested (in Middle English, as *legioun*) around 1200, from Old French *legion*, from Latin *legiō*, *legionem*, from *legō* (“to gather, collect”); akin to *legend*, *lecture*. which was borrowed from Spanish.

let's-do-a-quick-round-of-introductions.phonetic: /ˌlɛts du ə ˌkwɪk ˌɹaʊnd ʌv ˌɪntɹəˈdʌkʃənz/

senses.definition: Asking each person to introduce themselves briefly.

core.definition: A meeting phrase inviting each person in a group to briefly say their name and role before the discussion begins.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌlɛts du ə ˌkwɪk ˌɹaʊnd ʌv ˌɪntɹəˈdʌkʃənz/
pronunciation.respelling: lets doo uh kwik rownd uhv in-truh-DUK-shuhnz
pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on DUK in introductions, and 'round' is pronounced 'rownd' with a clear 'r'. Reduce 'a' to 'uh' and 'of' to 'uhv', and link the words so the phrase flows quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and welcoming. It sets a friendly, organized tone at the start of a meeting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase at the beginning of meetings, workshops, classes, or team calls, especially with new members. It is often followed by people stating their name, team, and one fact about themselves. A natural reply is simply to go first or say 'Sure, I'll start.'

distinctions.note: Quick intro is shorter and more informal; a quick round of introductions implies that everyone will take a turn.
Let's introduce ourselves is a direct invitation for the group; a quick round of introductions frames it as an organized process.

collocations: start with a round of introductions

examples.everyday: Since we have a few new neighbors at the block party, let's do a quick round of introductions.
examples.professional: Before we start the sprint review, let's do a quick round of introductions for our new analysts.
examples.analytical: The seminar begins with a quick round of introductions, which establishes the speakers' positions before the argument unfolds.

nuance.analogy: Like passing a microphone around a circle, each person gets a short turn to speak.
nuance.etymology: 'Introduction' comes from Latin 'introducere' (to lead in); 'round' here means a turn taken by each person in turn.
common_mistakes: Using 'a quick round of introduction' in the singular, which is less natural than the plural 'introductions'.
Pronouncing 'round' as 'rund' instead of 'rownd'.

conversation.text: We have some new faces today, so let's do a quick round of introductions.
Before we start, let's do a quick round of introductions: name and role.
Let's do a quick round of introductions. Ana, do you want to start?

senses.definition: The probability that some fixed outcome was generated by a random distribution with a specific parameter.
The probability of a specified outcome; the chance of something happening; probability; the state or degree of being probable.
senses.example: In all likelihood the meeting will be canceled.

senses.definition: Likeness, resemblance.

core.definition: The probability of observed data given specific parameter values in statistics; in everyday use, the chance that something will happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The last syllable is a short 'hood' with the vowel of 'good', not 'hoot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds precise and somewhat formal, and it is neutral in both everyday and technical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'likelihood' more in formal writing, analysis and business meetings, and 'chance' in casual talk. The phrase 'in all likelihood' is common in both spoken and written English. In statistics, likelihood has a specific meaning and is distinct from probability.

distinctions.note: Probability is the chance of an outcome given a model, while likelihood is how well a model's parameters explain observed data.
Chance is informal and everyday, while likelihood sounds more formal and precise.

examples.everyday: There's a good likelihood it'll rain, so bring an umbrella.
examples.professional: Based on the test results, there is a high likelihood that the new model will improve retention.
examples.analytical: The likelihood of the data under the proposed parameters is what justifies choosing that model over its rival.

nuance.analogy: Think of it as a dial that rates how well a story explains the evidence you already have.
nuance.etymology: From 'likely' plus '-hood', from Old English lician and the suffix -hād.
common_mistakes: Using 'likelihood to' with an infinitive; the usual pattern is 'the likelihood that' or 'the likelihood of'.
Misspelling it as 'likelyhood', which is a common error.
Treating likelihood and probability as synonyms in data science writing, where they have different meanings.

conversation.text: The likelihood measures how probable the observed data is under a given set of parameters.
There's a high likelihood the deadline will slip if the labels arrive late.
Our model achieves a higher test log-likelihood than the baseline.

senses.definition: A small parasitic wingless insect of the order Psocodea.
The currency sign ¤.
A contemptible person; one who is deceitful or causes harm.
To remove lice from; to delouse.

core.definition: A small wingless insect that lives on the skin or hair of people and animals and feeds on their blood.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with house and mouse, with a diphthong ow sound. The plural is lice, pronounced with a long i, which is a common mistake.

nuance.connotation: Negative; the insect itself is unpleasant, and as an insult it is mild but disrespectful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use louse for the insect, usually in talk about head lice in schools or health concerns. As an insult, you louse sounds old-fashioned and mildly harsh, and people more often say jerk or creep. Using it in a casual way may sound a bit dramatic or comic.

distinctions.note: A nit is the egg of a louse, while a louse is the adult insect.
A bedbug is a different insect that feeds on people at night, while a louse is a parasite of the hair or skin.

examples.everyday: The school sent a note home because a few kids had head lice, so check your child's hair tonight.
examples.professional: The clinic's health guidance on lice outbreaks is posted on the staff intranet.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers often used the louse as a symbol of human filth and vulnerability to sin.

nuance.analogy: A louse on a person is like an unwanted uninvited guest that lives in the house and never leaves.
nuance.etymology: From Old English lūs, from a Germanic root shared with German Laus.
common_mistakes: Saying the plural as louses, which is only used for the insulting sense; the insect's plural is lice.
Pronouncing lice with the vowel of rice instead of the long i of nice.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word kinnim (כִּנִּים) appears in the story of the third plague in Egypt in Exodus 8:16-18. The RSV translates it as gnats, though many other translations render it as lice. Psalm 105:31 also refers to these insects as part of the plagues. These passages show the insect as a sign of God's power over Egypt.

louse.etymology: From Middle English *lous*, *lows*, *lowse*, from Old English *lūs*, from **lūs*, from Proto-Germanic **lūs*, from Proto-Indo-European **lewH-*.

senses.definition: Suffering from malnutrition.

core.definition: Weak, unhealthy, or underdeveloped because the body has not received enough nutrients over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NUR, the second syllable, and the vowel in the middle is r-colored. The final -ished sounds like 'isht', and the word is not pronounced 'mal-NOR-ished'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious health problem, often in medical, nutritional, or humanitarian contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use malnourished for people, especially children, who are seriously underfed or who lack key nutrients. In everyday speech they may simply say 'undernourished' or 'not eating enough', and calling an adult malnourished can sound clinical. The word is common in news about hunger and health.

distinctions.note: Undernourished means not getting enough food, while malnourished means lacking proper nutrients, even if the person eats something.
Malnutrition is the noun for the condition, while malnourished is the adjective describing the person.

examples.everyday: The shelter volunteer said some of the dogs were badly malnourished when they arrived.
examples.professional: The clinic reports that many of the malnourished patients are children under five.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that a society can have plenty of food and still have malnourished populations because of inequality in access.

nuance.analogy: A malnourished body is like a car with a full tank of the wrong fuel: it runs, but it cannot function well.
nuance.etymology: From mal- meaning 'bad, ill' plus nourished, from Old French norrir, 'to feed, to raise'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'mal-NOR-ished' with a stressed 'or' vowel.
Using malnourished when you only mean that someone is hungry at the moment.

senses.definition: To enroll as a member of a body, especially of a college or university.
To join or enter (a group, body, category of people, etc.).
To be enrolled as a member of a body, especially of a college or university.
To graduate (from a school or course of study).
A person admitted to membership in a society or college.

core.definition: To enroll formally as a student at a college or university, or to be admitted to membership in an institution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRIK, the second syllable. Americans flap the t in the middle, making it sound closer to 'muh-TRIK.' The final -ate is pronounced 'ayt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and formal; it describes an official step, usually with a positive tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, matriculate is the usual formal term for officially enrolling in a college or university, as in 'She matriculated in the fall.' In everyday talk, people more often say 'enroll' or 'start school.' It is common on university websites and in announcements.

distinctions.note: Enroll is the everyday word for signing up for classes; matriculate is more formal and emphasizes official admission to the institution.
Graduate means completing a program; matriculate means beginning it.

examples.everyday: My son matriculates at the state university this fall, so we're finally getting him a dorm room.
examples.professional: Students who matriculate in the spring semester must complete the placement exam before registering for calculus.
examples.analytical: Medieval students who matriculated at a university swore an oath and entered a corporate community with its own rights.

nuance.analogy: Like stepping through a gate that officially welcomes you into a campus community.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin matriculare, to enroll, from matricula, a register, from Latin matrix, register or womb.
common_mistakes: Using matriculate with a direct object, as in 'he matriculated the school'; it is intransitive, so use 'matriculate at' or 'matriculate into.'
Confusing matriculate with graduate; matriculate means starting, while graduate means finishing.

matriculate.etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1487, in Middle English, the verb in 1557; Latin *mātrīculātus*, perfect passive participle of *mātrīculō* (“to register”) (see *-ate*), from *mātrīcula* (“public register”), a diminutive of Latin *mātrīx* (“list”).

senses.definition: The act or state of being a mendicant.

core.definition: The condition or practice of living by begging, especially as a member of a religious order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MEN. The second syllable is a reduced 'ih', and the final -cy is 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing a historical or religious practice; can sound negative when it describes poverty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in history, religious studies, and literature. It is not an everyday word. In ordinary speech people say 'begging' or 'living on charity'.

distinctions.note: Begging is the everyday word for asking for money or food. Mendicancy is the formal term for the state or practice of living by begging.
Mendicity is a less common synonym that is also formal; mendicancy is used more often in religious and historical writing.

examples.everyday: My grandmother said that begging on the street was a kind of mendicancy she never wanted to fall into.
examples.professional: Our grant proposal should avoid any impression of mendicancy and focus on our research results.
examples.analytical: Medieval reformers debated whether mendicancy was a faithful form of poverty or a dependence on others' charity.

nuance.analogy: Mendicancy is like a bird that never builds its own nest and survives only on what others leave out for it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mendicare, to beg.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'dee' (men-DI-kan-see). The middle vowel is reduced.
Confusing it with 'mendacity', which means lying.

senses.definition: Deserving of merit or commendation; deserving reward.
senses.example: The policeman received the Award of Meritorious Service from his grateful department.

core.definition: Deserving praise, recognition, or reward because of the quality of effort, achievement or conduct.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TOR, with a clear American r. The ending '-ious' is reduced to 'ee-us', not 'ee-oos'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone's effort or achievement in a formal way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'meritorious' in awards, official commendations, military citations and academic praise, such as 'meritorious service.' In casual speech, 'great' or 'worthy' is more natural. It sounds stiff if used for small everyday things, so save it for serious recognition.

distinctions.note: Praiseworthy is common and general; meritorious is more formal and suggests that the thing deserves an official reward or award.
Commendable is close in meaning but more everyday; meritorious implies deserving a formal honor.

examples.everyday: Your work at the food bank has been meritorious, and the whole neighborhood appreciates it.
examples.professional: The committee nominated her for the award because her analysis showed meritorious leadership on the project.
examples.analytical: Aristotle argues that a virtuous action is meritorious only when it is chosen for its own sake and not merely for reward.

nuance.analogy: Like a gold star that a teacher gives after careful work: it marks the effort as deserving more than a passing nod.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin meritorius, from Latin meritum, 'merit, deserving'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'meh-RIT-or-ee-us' with stress on the wrong syllable.
Confusing it with 'meretricious', which means flashy and cheap.

meritorious.etymology: From Middle English *meritorious*, borrowed between 1375 and 1425 from Latin *meritōrius* (“earning money”), from *meritus*, past participle of *mereō* (“to earn”).

senses.definition: In the Bible, a prophet of Judah in the late 8th century BC, and the author of the book of Micah, who condemned social injustice and predicted the fall of Jerusalem and Samaria.

core.definition: In the Bible, a prophet of Judah in the late 8th century BC, and the author of the book of Micah, who condemned social injustice and predicted the fall of Jerusalem and Samaria.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a soft 'uh', as in 'sofa'. Do not say 'MEE-kah', which is a common error from Spanish or Italian.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In religious settings it signals a respected prophet.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches, Bible studies and seminaries, 'Micah' is said naturally, and the book is cited as 'Micah' in sermons. Outside religious contexts it is mostly a given name. Americans would normally say 'the book of Micah' rather than 'the prophet Micah' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: 'Micah' is the standard spelling for the prophet and the book; 'Mica' is a spelling variant that appears in some versions and in given names.
'Micaiah' is a different prophet, son of Imlah, who appears in 1 Kings 22; the two names are related but not the same person.

examples.everyday: Have you ever read Micah? There's a verse about doing justice and walking humbly that my pastor always quotes.
examples.professional: For the sermon series, we'll read Micah on Sunday evening and tie it to the Old Testament survey.
examples.analytical: Micah's oracles against social injustice in Jerusalem and Samaria are central to any study of the eighth-century prophets.

nuance.analogy: Micah is like a country preacher who speaks plainly to the city's rich and powerful about their unfairness.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Mikhayahu, 'who is like Yahweh', shortened to Mikhah.
common_mistakes: Saying 'MEE-kah' instead of 'MY-kuh'.
Confusing the prophet Micah with Micaiah, a different prophet in 1 Kings 22.
nuance.biblical_note: Micah (Hebrew Mikhah, 'who is like Yahweh') was a prophet from Moresheth in Judah, active in the time of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the place from which a ruler will come. Micah 6:8 summarizes what the Lord requires: justice, kindness and a humble walk with God. Micah 3:12 announces that Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins, a warning Jeremiah later recalls in Jeremiah 26:18.

senses.definition: In AI: When an AI system's goals or behavior differ from what its developers or users intended.
The state, or an instance, of being misaligned.

core.definition: A state in which an AI system's goals or behavior differ from what its designers or users intended.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'line', not on 'mis'. Reduce the 'a' in the second syllable to a quick schwa sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a technical problem to be fixed, often with some concern about safety.
nuance.usage_note: In American AI research and industry, 'misalignment' is a standard term used in papers, safety discussions, and product meetings. Outside tech and policy, people would more likely say 'mismatch' or 'out of sync'. It is used both for AI systems and for general organizational alignment problems.

distinctions.note: 'Mismatch' describes two things that do not fit together, while 'misalignment' often refers to goals or values drifting apart.
'Misspecification' means the objective was written incorrectly, while 'misalignment' describes the resulting gap between intended and actual behavior.

examples.everyday: My phone's voice assistant keeps doing the wrong thing, so there's clearly some misalignment in how it understands me.
examples.professional: We found a misalignment between the model's optimization target and what the business team actually wanted to measure.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that misalignment becomes more dangerous as systems gain autonomy and their goals are harder to inspect.

nuance.analogy: It is like a GPS that gives perfectly confident directions to the wrong address: it works, but it is pursuing the wrong goal.
nuance.etymology: From 'mis-' (wrongly) plus 'alignment' (arrangement in a line).
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on 'mis' instead of 'line'.
Using 'misalignment' for a simple software bug where 'error' or 'bug' is more natural.

conversation.text: Misalignment is when a system's behavior diverges from what its designers intended.
Optimizing for engagement instead of user well-being is a familiar form of misalignment.
There's some misalignment between the product and research teams on what "done" means.

senses.definition: An architecture in which a router sends each input (in language models, each token) to a few of many specialist subnetworks, so only part of the model runs each time.

core.definition: An AI model design in which a router sends each input to a few specialist subnetworks out of many, so only part of the model runs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the main word 'EX-perts' and say 'of' as a weak uhv. The 'ture' in mixture is pronounced 'chur', so the whole first word has a ch sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a technical architecture term, positive in discussions of efficiency.
nuance.usage_note: In American AI research and industry, mixture of experts (often abbreviated MoE) describes large language models where a router picks a few experts per token. People say 'MoE model' in meetings and papers. It is a technical term, so use the full phrase with careful explanation outside experts' circles.

distinctions.note: An ensemble runs several complete models and combines their outputs; mixture of experts runs only a few parts of one model for each input.
A dense model uses all its parameters for every input; a mixture of experts model activates only a few experts each time.

collocations: top-k gating in mixture of experts

examples.everyday: My friend says the new chatbot uses a mixture of experts model.
examples.professional: Switching to a mixture of experts layer lets us grow capacity without raising per-token compute.
examples.analytical: A mixture of experts model separates capacity from computation: total parameters grow while each token activates only a few.

nuance.analogy: Like a hospital where each patient sees only the two specialists they need, instead of every doctor examining everyone.
nuance.etymology: Mixture from Latin mixtura, a mingling; expert from Latin expertus, having tried or experienced.
common_mistakes: Saying 'mixture of expert' with a singular noun; the standard phrase uses the plural 'experts'.
Confusing it with ensemble methods, which combine whole models rather than routing inputs.

conversation.text: In a mixture of experts layer, a router sends each token to a few expert subnetworks.
Mixture of experts lets the model have many parameters while using only a fraction of them for each token.
Mixture of experts saves compute per token, but serving it needs memory for all the experts.

senses.definition: Especially of a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.: intended to help in remembering.
Of or relating to mnemonics (“the study of techniques for remembering anything more easily”).
Of or relating to memory.
Something (especially a series of ideas, letters, words, etc.) used to help in remembering a thing; a memory aid.
The human-readable, textual form of an assembly language instruction, not including operands.
Synonym of mnemonics (“the study of techniques for remembering anything more easily”).

core.definition: A memory aid, such as a rhyme, acronym or phrase, that helps you remember something.

pronunciation.tip: The initial M is silent, so start with the 'nuh' sound. The stress falls on the second syllable, MAH. Watch the reduced first vowel, which is a quick schwa sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is praised as a helpful learning tool, and teachers commonly recommend it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mnemonic' mostly in school, medicine, music and test prep, as in 'a mnemonic for the planets.' A typical situation is a teacher saying, 'Here's a mnemonic to help you remember.' In everyday talk, people more often say 'a trick' or 'a way to remember,' so 'mnemonic' sounds slightly technical there.

distinctions.note: 'Mnemonic' is usually the memory aid itself, while 'mnemonics' is the field or set of techniques for remembering.
To memorize means to learn something by heart; a mnemonic is a tool that helps you do that.

examples.everyday: My daughter taught me a silly mnemonic for the order of the colors in a rainbow, and it actually works.
examples.professional: Let's add a mnemonic to the onboarding guide so new hires remember the four escalation levels.
examples.analytical: A mnemonic works by attaching arbitrary material to a structure the learner already knows, which is why rhymes and vivid images improve recall.

nuance.analogy: A mnemonic is like a sticky note on the inside of your head: it does not store the information, but it shows you where to find it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek mnēmonikos, 'relating to memory,' from mnēmōn, 'mindful.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent M ('m-nuh-mon-ik').
Using 'mnemonic' as a verb; the correct verb is 'memorize' or 'remember'.

mnemonic.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin *mnemonicus* or its etymon Ancient Greek *μνημονῐκός* (“pertaining to memory or remembrance, memorial”) + *-ic*.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to the modality between propositions.
Relating to the form of a thing rather to any of its attributes.
Of, or relating to a mode or modus.
Of, relating to, or describing the mood of a clause.
Relating to the statistical mode.
Having separate modes in which user input has different effects.
Requiring immediate user interaction and thus presented so that it cannot be closed or interacted behind until a decision is made.
senses.example: a modal dialog; a modal window

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or composed in the musical modi by which an octave is divided, associated with emotional moods in Ancient — and in medieval ecclesiastical — music.
In a mode which is not major or minor scale, the standard modes used in the Western musical tradition.
A modal (etymology 1, adjective sense 4) proposition.
A modal (etymology 1, adjective sense 2) form, notably a modal auxiliary.
A modal verb.
A modal (etymology 1, adjective sense 7) window, one that cannot be closed until a decision is made.
A semi-synthetic fabric, a very soft kind of rayon textile made from beech tree pulp and processed with chemicals.

core.definition: Relating to modality, that is, to whether a statement is necessarily, possibly or contingently true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'dul', not 'dell'. Do not confuse it with 'model', which is a different word in pronunciation as well as meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In logic and philosophy, Americans use 'modal' to talk about necessity and possibility. In grammar, Americans say 'modal verb' or 'modal auxiliary' for words like 'can', 'must' and 'should'. In data science, 'modal' can also describe the most frequent value, though most people say 'mode' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Modular' means built from separate parts; 'modal' concerns necessity and possibility or grammatical mood.
'Categorical' is the contrasting logical term for statements that are not qualified by necessity or possibility.

examples.everyday: My grammar teacher said 'must' and 'should' are modal verbs.
examples.professional: The spec distinguishes modal requirements, which must hold, from ordinary requirements.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's modal syllogisms treat necessity and possibility as qualifiers of the premises.

nuance.analogy: A modal claim is like a weather forecast: it does not say what happened, but what could or must happen.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'modalis', from 'modus', meaning measure or manner.
common_mistakes: Saying 'model' for 'modal'; they are pronounced differently.
Using 'modal' as a noun for grammar without saying 'modal verb'.

senses.definition: In AI: Continuously tracking a deployed model's performance, inputs and outputs to catch problems.
The carrying out of surveillance on, or continuous or regular observation of, an environment or people in order to detect signals, movements or changes of state or quality.

core.definition: In AI, the continuous tracking of a deployed model's performance, inputs and outputs to catch problems early.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the middle syllables are reduced. The r in the third syllable is strongly rhotic, and the final ing is unstressed, not a long EE sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral: it describes a routine practice, positive when it prevents failures.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say monitoring in data science and operations teams to mean watching a live system for drift, errors or latency. In everyday speech it can also mean watching a child or a health condition. Teams often say 'model monitoring' or 'production monitoring' to be precise.

distinctions.note: Evaluation measures a model before release; monitoring watches it continuously after deployment.
Observability is the broader ability to understand a system from its outputs; monitoring is the practice of watching specific signals.

examples.everyday: My aunt has heart monitoring at home, so her doctor gets a report every morning.
examples.professional: After the launch, the team added monitoring for input drift so we would notice when the model starts failing.
examples.analytical: Effective monitoring of machine learning systems requires tracking not only accuracy but also the distribution of inputs over time.

nuance.analogy: Like a smoke detector for a model, monitoring warns you before a small problem becomes a fire.
nuance.etymology: From Latin monere, to warn or remind.
common_mistakes: Using monitoring as a countable noun; say 'monitoring' or 'a monitoring system'.
Pronouncing the second syllable as MON; it is reduced to a short i.

conversation.text: Monitoring tracks latency, error rates, and output quality once the model is live.
We use automated monitoring to flag possible misuse in API traffic.
Monitoring caught a spike in refusals right after the prompt change.

senses.definition: A person who obstinately adheres to old ways in spite of clear evidence that they are wrong; an ignorant and bigoted opponent of reform.
An obvious error that is obstinately repeated despite correction.

core.definition: A person or belief that stubbornly clings to an old error even after being shown the correct version.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -sim- and -mus endings are weak and quick. The word is rare, so you will mainly see it in writing and in discussions of history or language.

nuance.connotation: negative. It mocks stubbornness and refusal to accept correction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in speech; it appears in essays, books on language, and scholarly writing, often to mock someone who insists on an obvious mistake. It is not a slur, but calling someone a mumpsimus in a meeting would sound pedantic and unkind. A more common everyday equivalent is 'stubborn as a mule' or simply 'set in their ways.'

distinctions.note: A dinosaur is an older person or outdated thing that is past its time; a mumpsimus specifically holds on to a known error.
A stick-in-the-mud is informal and resists change generally; a mumpsimus is literary and clings to a specific error.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still insists that the Earth is the only planet, and he's a real mumpsimus about it.
examples.professional: In the review, the editor was a mumpsimus who kept rejecting the corrected formula no matter what the data showed.
examples.analytical: The historian argued that the scholars were mumpsimuses, obstinately defending a mistranslation long after the original text had been checked.

nuance.analogy: A mumpsimus is like a GPS that keeps sending you down a closed road after the map has been corrected, because the driver refuses to believe the update.
nuance.etymology: From a medieval priest's mistaken Latin phrase 'mumpsimus' in place of 'sumpsimus', a story popularized by Erasmus.
common_mistakes: Using it for any mistake; it describes stubborn refusal to correct an error, not an honest mistake.
Writing 'mumsimus' or 'mumpsimous' as an adjective; the noun is the usual form.

mumpsimus.etymology: Malapropism of Latin *sumpsimus*, form of *sūmō* (“to take”), from a story of an old monk who misrecited the Eucharist with quod in ōre mumpsimus instead of quod in ōre sumpsimus “which we have taken into the mouth”, and stubbornly continued using the…

senses.definition: Finding and labeling names of people, places, organizations and the like in text.

core.definition: A natural language processing task in which a program finds words or phrases that name people, places, organizations, dates or products in text and labels each one with its category.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on NAYMD and EN in the first two words, with NISH carrying the strongest stress of the last word. Say the first t in 'entity' as a flap, so it sounds like 'EN-tih-tee', and do not pronounce the r in 'entity' as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge, though it appears in discussions of privacy because the task can expose personal information.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers use this term in papers, code reviews, and project meetings, usually shortened to NER. Americans say it in full at first mention and then use the abbreviation. Outside technical settings, most people would not use the phrase.

distinctions.note: Entity extraction is a broader term that can include linking entities to a knowledge base; named entity recognition specifically means detecting and classifying the names in text.
Text classification assigns a label to a whole document or sentence, while named entity recognition labels individual spans of words inside the text.

collocations: train a named entity recognition system
entity types such as person and organization

examples.everyday: My friend is building a tool that uses named entity recognition to pull company names out of news articles, and she says it works surprisingly well.
examples.professional: Our team will deploy the named entity recognition model to the customer support pipeline next sprint, after we finish the accuracy tests.
examples.analytical: A named entity recognition system encodes a theory of what counts as a name, and that theory shapes which people and places become visible in the resulting data.

nuance.analogy: It works like a highlighter that marks every proper name on a page and writes a small tag beside each one, such as PERSON or PLACE.
nuance.etymology: 'Entity' comes from Late Latin 'entitas', from Latin 'ens' meaning being; 'named' means having a name.
common_mistakes: Saying 'entity name recognition' or 'name entity recognition', which are not standard terms; use 'named entity recognition'.
Stressing 'ENtity' and 'recognition' evenly, which makes the phrase sound flat; the main stresses are on the first word and on NISH.
Confusing it with 'named entity linking', which connects a found name to a specific record in a database.

conversation.text: Named entity recognition finds and labels names of people, organizations, places, and dates in text.
We use named entity recognition to redact patient names before the data leaves the hospital.
General-purpose named entity recognition misses drug names, so we trained a domain-specific model.

senses.definition: A form or state of connection.
A connected group; a network, a web.
A center or focus of something.
In the work of the Danish linguist Otto Jespersen (1860–1943): a group of words expressing two concepts in one unit (such as a clause or sentence).
The relationship between a vendor and a jurisdiction for the purpose of taxation, established for example by the vendor operating a physical store in that jurisdiction.
A person who had contracted a nexum or obligation of such a kind that, if they failed to pay, their creditor could compel them to work as a servant until the debt was paid; an indentured servant.

core.definition: A central connection or link that brings together several related people, things, or ideas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'suss', not 'sus' or 'sooss'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a point where things connect, and it can sound slightly elevated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nexus mostly in writing, academic or policy discussions, and business analysis. In casual speech people usually say connection, link, or center. Do not use it for a simple one-to-one link; it implies a network of related things.

distinctions.note: A connection is a simple link, while a nexus is a central point where many connections meet.
A hub is a physical or organizational center, while nexus can be abstract, such as a nexus of ideas or causes.

examples.everyday: Our town is the nexus for three bus lines, so everyone ends up passing through downtown.
examples.professional: Our team sits at the nexus of product and data, so we see the problems from both sides.
examples.analytical: The essay locates the nexus between faith and reason in the question of what counts as evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a major railway junction where many lines meet, the nexus is where many routes converge.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nexus, past participle of nectere, 'to bind or tie together'.
common_mistakes: Using nexus for an ordinary link, where connection is more natural.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full vowel, as in NEK-sus with a long u.

nexus.etymology: From Latin *nexus* (“connection, nexus; act of binding, tying or fastening together; something which binds, binding, bond, fastening, joint; legal obligation”), from *nectō* (“to attach, bind, connect, fasten, tie; to interweave; to relate; to unite; to…

senses.definition: Of or relating to nihilism.

core.definition: Relating to nihilism, the belief that life has no inherent meaning, value, or moral truth, or that nothing can be known or justified.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LIS, the second syllable of the stem nihil-ist. Many Americans say NIE-uh-list-ik, so the first vowel is often a long I sound; avoid stressing the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes a bleak or dismissive worldview, and it can sound like an accusation if applied to a person's attitude without qualification.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nihilistic mostly in philosophy, literature, culture criticism, and political commentary, for example 'a nihilistic view of history'. In casual speech people more often say someone is cynical, hopeless, or 'don't care about anything'. Calling a person nihilistic can sound harsh, so use it carefully about real people.

distinctions.note: Cynical means distrustful of people's motives; nihilistic goes further and denies that any values or meanings are justified at all.
Pessimistic expects bad outcomes, while nihilistic rejects the idea that outcomes or actions have any ultimate meaning.

examples.everyday: My roommate has been pretty nihilistic lately, saying nothing we do really matters.
examples.professional: The product team worried that the user survey showed a nihilistic mood, with customers feeling their feedback changes nothing.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche's critique of morality is often read as a nihilistic diagnosis, yet he presented it as a prelude to new values rather than their absence.

nuance.analogy: A nihilistic view is like a map with every road erased: it claims there is nowhere worth going.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nihil, 'nothing', through the 19th-century German term Nihilismus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (NI-hi-lis-tik) instead of the middle syllable LIS.
Using nihilistic as a synonym for 'depressed' or 'sad' in everyday speech, when it refers to a philosophical denial of meaning.

senses.definition: Casual: I'm surprised; I can't believe it.

core.definition: A casual exclamation meaning you are very surprised, or that you refuse to do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WAY, and the vowel is a clear diphthong that ends in a short ee sound. Keep 'no' short and relaxed before it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lively; it can express delighted surprise or firm refusal, depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it casually when hearing big news ('No way! You got the job?') or when refusing a request ('No way am I going to that party'). Tone decides the meaning. It is informal, so avoid it in professional writing or serious conversations.

distinctions.note: No way, José is playful and dated; ordinary No way! is more common and neutral.
No way out means there is no escape; No way! is a reaction or refusal.

examples.everyday: You won the raffle at the church picnic? No way!
examples.professional: The vendor says the system can be ready by Friday. No way, that timeline isn't realistic.
examples.analytical: The phrase no way conveys both incredulity and refusal, showing how a single expression can carry surprise and rejection at once.

nuance.analogy: Like a sudden jolt that makes you stop and blink, whether from joy or from refusal.
common_mistakes: Using it as a neutral question about a way or route; it is an exclamation in conversation.
Overusing it as a flat refusal in professional talk, where a softer 'I don't think that will work' is better.

conversation.text: "I won the raffle!" "No way! What did you win?"
No way! You know my cousin?
"Can you work this weekend?" "No way. I've had plans for months."

senses.definition: The number or expression written above the line in a fraction (such as 1 in ½).
An enumerator; someone who counts.

core.definition: The number written above the line in a fraction, showing how many parts of the whole are being counted.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NOO, with a lighter secondary stress on -RAY. The final -ator is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so do not stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a neutral math term used in classrooms and technical settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans learn this word in elementary school, usually with the phrase 'top number' as a memory aid. It is used in math class, cooking, and technical work. In casual talk, people often just say 'the top number' or 'the top of the fraction.'

distinctions.note: The numerator is the top number, showing how many parts you have, while the denominator is the bottom number, showing how many equal parts make the whole.
A numeral is a symbol representing a number, while the numerator is a specific position in a fraction.

examples.everyday: Wait, which number is the numerator, the top one or the bottom one?
examples.professional: The numerator counts successful API calls, and the denominator counts total requests, so the ratio is our error-free rate.
examples.analytical: When the numerator and denominator share a common factor, the fraction reduces to lowest terms without changing its value.

nuance.analogy: Like counting the slices of pizza you eat (the numerator) out of the total number of slices (the denominator).
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin numerator, 'counter', from Latin numerare, 'to count'.
common_mistakes: Reversing the numerator and denominator, especially when reading fractions aloud.
Stressing the last syllable; say NOO-muh-ray-ter, not noo-muh-RAY-ter.

senses.definition: To shade; to darken; to cloud.
Lying under some projecting part, like the abdomen of certain spiders.

core.definition: To cast a shadow over something or make it dark, dim, or hard to see.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable 'um,' not the first. The vowel in the second syllable is short, like the 'u' in 'cup.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes darkening or obscuring, and it can have a poetic or somber tone.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, bookish word that Americans would encounter in older literature or scholarly texts. In everyday speech, say 'darken,' 'shade,' or 'cloud over.' The adjective sense, meaning lying under a projecting part, appears in biology and entomology.

distinctions.note: Shade is common and everyday. Obumbrate is rare and literary, and it suggests a more deliberate or mysterious darkening.
Obscure means to make something hard to understand or see. Obumbrate focuses on the physical act of casting shadow.

examples.everyday: Those tall pines really obumbrate the back porch by late afternoon, so we never get much sun there.
examples.professional: The new building will obumbrate the plaza, so we should review the sunlight study before approval.
examples.analytical: Some medieval theologians described sin as a veil that obumbrates the divine light within the soul.

nuance.analogy: Like a passing cloud that dims a bright field, obumbrate describes a shadow falling gently over something.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obumbrare, 'to overshadow,' from ob- 'over' plus umbrare 'to shade.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Using obumbrate in casual speech where 'shade' or 'darken' would be natural.

obumbrate.etymology: Latin *obumbrātus*, of *obumbrō* (“to overshadow, cloud”), from *ob* + *umbrō*; see *-ate* and *-ate*.

senses.definition: Being everywhere simultaneously.

core.definition: Seeming to be everywhere at the same time; present or found in all places, often in a way that feels constant or unavoidable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PREZ, the third syllable. The final syllable is a reduced uhnt, not ent with a clear e sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative in everyday talk, suggesting something that is everywhere and unavoidable, such as advertising, screens, or stress. In theology, it is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use omnipresent in news, business, and everyday complaints, such as omnipresent advertising or omnipresent smartphones. It can be used about God in religious settings, but in ordinary conversation it is a little formal. Americans usually say everywhere or all over for a simpler tone.

distinctions.note: Ubiquitous is the more common word for things found everywhere, especially in business and technology writing; omnipresent often carries a sense of something oppressive or constant.
Present means being in a place now or existing at a time; omnipresent means being everywhere at once, to an extreme degree.

examples.everyday: Ads are omnipresent on my phone, so I started using a blocker just to get some peace.
examples.professional: Our team saw that security warnings had become omnipresent in the dashboard, so users stopped reading them.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that surveillance technologies are now omnipresent, shaping behavior even when no one is actively monitoring anyone.

nuance.analogy: Omnipresent is like background music in a store: once it is everywhere, you notice it only when it stops.
nuance.etymology: From Latin omnipraesens, from omnis (all) and praesens (present).
common_mistakes: Using omnipresent for something that is only sometimes everywhere; it means present everywhere, so it is strong.
Pronouncing the final syllable as ent with a full vowel; it is reduced.

senses.definition: Bijective or injective.
Involving one attacker and one defender.
In a one-on-one manner.
senses.example: He was willing to go one-on-one with the District Attorney himself.

senses.definition: A contest involving only one player on each side, especially of an activity often involving teams.
senses.example: Why don't we play a little one-on-one until the others show up.

core.definition: Involving just two people, one on one, such as a private meeting or conversation between a manager and an employee.

pronunciation.tip: The middle word 'on' is reduced to 'ahn' or 'un' and is nearly silent. The strongest stress falls on the final 'one', so say it as 'wun-un-WUN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting personal attention and focus.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'one-on-one' a lot at work for a regular meeting between a manager and a direct report, and in sports for a head-to-head contest. As a noun or adverb, 'have a one-on-one' or 'we talked one-on-one' is natural. A natural reply to 'Can we do a one-on-one?' is 'Sure, what time works?'

distinctions.note: 'One-on-one' is the everyday workplace and social term. 'One-to-one' is more formal and is also used in math and sales.
A group meeting includes several people, while a one-on-one involves only two people.
